content: Treatment services for tuberculosis (TB) are delivered by the National TB Programme (NTP) through a network of public and private healthcare facilities. In August 2021, a dual screening and testing model for TB and COVID-19 was introduced in Manila to address the decline in TB case notifications. The development and implementation of this model were guided by multiple assessments conducted collaboratively by academic institutions, international organizations, and the Ministry of Health. These assessments included a modeling study on the impact of COVID-19 on achieving national TB notification targets, an analysis of TB notification rates before and after the introduction of community quarantine, and a rapid assessment of the impact of COVID-19 on TB service delivery. To secure political commitment and stakeholder engagement, the findings from these assessments were presented to key stakeholders, including local government officials, health facility managers, and TB laboratory representatives. TB screening was offered to all individuals attending COVID-19 swabbing facilities, and TB testing was provided to individuals with confirmed COVID-19 who were admitted to isolation facilities. Stakeholder roles and responsibilities were clearly defined prior to implementation, and communication campaigns were designed to raise public awareness and encourage the use of these services. Additional laboratory staff were recruited to perform Xpert MTB/RIF testing, and field teams received ongoing mentoring and support. Monitoring and evaluation systems were established, with regular on-site and remote joint monitoring activities conducted by technical and operational teams. A project-specific database was used to record real-time updates, and TB notifications were integrated into the NTP’s TB information system. Indicators such as the number of individuals screened and diagnosed with TB were reviewed during regular meetings involving technical and operational teams, the Manila Health Department NTP team, and other stakeholders. During the first two months of implementation, 1,106 individuals underwent symptom-based TB screening at COVID-19 swabbing facilities, of whom 889 were further screened using chest X-rays. Among these, 243 individuals underwent Xpert MTB/RIF testing, and 11 were diagnosed with TB. In isolation facilities, 404 individuals were tested for TB, and 5 were diagnosed with the disease. Key lessons learned included the importance of using multiple complementary assessments to identify gaps and secure political commitment. Close collaboration with stakeholders, including local government, COVID-19 facility managers, TB laboratories, and TB service providers, facilitated the integration of TB screening and testing within COVID-19 services. Public communication and health education activities were instrumental in increasing awareness and generating demand for these services. Operational and implementation research is critical for improving people-centered services. Recommended actions include identifying research priorities for TB and comorbidities based on data and evidence gaps, assessing the financial burden of TB and comorbidities on affected individuals and the health system, evaluating the cost-effectiveness of alternative integrated care models, and exploring the contribution of comorbidities to TB disease burden and mortality, including emerging threats like COVID-19. Strengthening operational and implementation research at all levels is essential to address challenges and develop effective solutions. Additionally, funding applications and proposals for research and economic analyses should be developed in collaboration with TB and related services, informed by national evaluation results. Research findings should be translated into revised and strengthened policies, programs, and service delivery frameworks.
